definitions.meaning: to rag someone is to tease them, so the past tense fits
dressed in rags — frayed and torn

explanation.walkthrough: The comma is the split. 'Rag' as a verb — the same rag as a student rag week — means to tease or torment, and the tatty clothing is there to bury that sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragged means tormented by teasing in one sense and dressed in torn rags in the other — two lives of the noun 'rag'.

parts.note: the sheep of the parable, taken as a ram
where the strayed animal is once it is found — safely home

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is one picture rather than two synonyms, and the question mark is the setter admitting it: the parable's sheep, back where it belongs.
explanation.definitionFit: To ram a point home is to drive it in until it cannot be missed — the battering-ram metaphor English keeps for forceful emphasis.

definitions.note: 'Bill' is not a synonym at all: it identifies the answer through Microsoft's Bill Gates, so a man's first name stands in for a plural noun.

definitions.meaning: what you open to walk into a garden

explanation.walkthrough: Five letters and a capital B, and the clue never says a person is involved. A bare first name is the setter's standing notice that a surname is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Garden gates are the plainest of features, while 'Bill' reaches the same word through the best-known man to carry it as a surname.

clue.text: Eating out as an artistic activity

definitions.meaning: acid biting into a metal plate eats the surface away
the printmaker's craft, and the print it produces

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a restaurant meal; the setter means chemistry. Both halves are -ing nouns, which is what lets one replace the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To etch is to corrode a surface away with acid, so 'eating out' is literal chemistry, and the same word names the printmaking art it serves.

definitions.note: The cricket call is plural in form but names one moment, the close of a day's play, so a singular definition of it is fair.
definitions.meaning: the umpire's call when a day's cricket finishes
a question that leaves you with nothing to say does this to you

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket supplies the noun and everyday speech the verb; the join is 'is', which quietly turns the second half into a definition of what the answer does.
explanation.definitionFit: Stumps is the umpire's word for the close of a day's cricket, and to stump somebody is to leave them with nothing to say.

clue.text: A penny accepted by ticket seller to leave the Tube

parts.note: a tout is who sells you a ticket outside the ground; he does the accepting
A, then P for penny — the pair go inside

explanation.walkthrough: P for penny is standing crossword furniture and 'accepted by' is the container signal. Tapping out is what an Oyster card does at the barrier on the way out.
explanation.definitionFit: To tap out is to touch your card on the reader as you exit the Underground, so the definition names a London action rather than offering a synonym.

parts.note: it straddles the gap between the two words: MorMONSIGNORe

explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' is the quietest hidden-word marker there is, and a religious surface makes the religious answer feel like a coincidence rather than a signpost.
explanation.definitionFit: A monsignor is a senior Roman Catholic priest given an honorary title by the Pope — a dignitary of that church in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Girl from South America banned, leaving the borders

parts.note: the compass abbreviation
the States, abbreviated
bANNEd without its outer B and D

explanation.walkthrough: 'From South America' looks like one place and is really two abbreviations laid end to end. 'Borders' means the first and last letters — a deletion worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: Susanne is a girl's name, the German and Scandinavian spelling of Susan, so the definition works by example rather than by meaning.

clue.text: To keep smooth, shave, then change: utter bliss

parts.note: to even something is to keep it smooth; those four letters join the fodder
nine more letters, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: One chunk of the fodder has to be translated before anything can be shuffled — 'keep smooth' becomes EVEN — and the colon fences the definition off at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Seventh heaven is the topmost heaven of Islamic and Jewish tradition, and being in it is the standing idiom for perfect happiness.

parts.note: love is nothing — the tennis zero
the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

explanation.walkthrough: Love for zero and MIT for university are two of the most reused pieces of crossword furniture; knowing them turns this into a two-second clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To omit something is to fail to do it — 'he omitted to mention it' is 'he failed to mention it' — so the two verbs swap cleanly.

parts.note: not the American state and not Woolf: the setter means the vine on the wall, and leaves you to supply its second word
read straight — the abstract noun for whatever makes your skin crawl

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines, with a pun holding it up: the plant is the Virginia creeper, and the question mark is the setter owning the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality of anything eerie is that it makes your skin crawl, and the Virginia creeper is the plant that supplies the word behind the pun.

clue.text: A pretentious type rejected one little-grown tree

parts.note: A SNOB is a pretentious type, and 'rejected' turns the whole phrase round
the Roman numeral

explanation.walkthrough: The 'A' at the head of the clue is fodder, not filler: it travels with the snob when the reversal happens, and that is what makes six letters land.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonsai is a miniature tree kept dwarfed in a shallow pot, so 'little-grown' describes how it is cultivated rather than which species it is.

clue.text: Bubbling tureen is making us very hungry

parts.note: the eight letters of TUREEN IS, stirred

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bubbling' does double duty: a pot on the stove for the surface, an instruction to stir eight letters for the solver. The 'is' is fodder, not grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: Esurient is the bookish word for hungry, from the Latin for 'about to eat', so the definition is a plain synonym in a rare register.

clue.text: Isolate small wader scratching back at barrier

parts.note: the clothes-label abbreviation
the wader is an EGRET, scratched at the back
a gate bars the way

explanation.walkthrough: The wader has to be the egret — a heron leaves the wrong letters — and 'scratching back' docks its tail. 'At' is holding the two halves together, nothing more.
explanation.definitionFit: To segregate is to keep groups apart from one another, which is isolating them by policy rather than by accident of geography.

clue.text: Feeling unwell, throw off outdoor coat

parts.note: feeling rough is feeling off-colour
to cast is to throw — you cast off, cast a line

explanation.walkthrough: 'Coat' is the trap: no garment is involved. Roughcast is the pebbly render put on an outside wall, and the traditional way to apply it really is to throw it.
explanation.definitionFit: Roughcast is the coarse plaster rendering spread over an outside wall, so 'coat' means a layer of covering, as in a coat of paint.

clue.text: One submissively bent is taken to offer respect

definitions.meaning: the joint that bends when a subject submits, as before a feudal lord
the modern gesture of solidarity lowers this same joint to the ground

explanation.walkthrough: English has two idioms about the same joint and they point opposite ways — one is a subject's surrender, the other a deliberate public statement. The clue splits at 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bending the knee has meant submission since feudal times, while taking the knee is the recent gesture of solidarity and respect.

parts.note: 'so tired' is 'very tired'
the country's own abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: No indicator at all — the shortest kind of charade, where refusing to read 'Very British' as one phrase is the whole battle.
explanation.definitionFit: A souk is the covered market of an Arab city, so 'marketplace' names it by its plainest category — it is the Arabic word for the same thing.

parts.note: a bridge spans a gap — a span
art in the sense of craft, tucked inside

explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is the smallest container indicator in the language and the easiest to read as ordinary English. Sparta's soldiers gave their name to going without.
explanation.definitionFit: Spartan means bare and austere — plain living with no comforts — which is 'simple' in the sense of unadorned rather than easy.

clue.text: Rehearsal for musical that has prearranged result?

definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause rather than a noun: the setter describes the answer — a trial whose verdict is settled in advance — instead of naming it.

parts.note: a musical is a show
a trial run is a rehearsal

explanation.walkthrough: The pieces arrive in the wrong order on purpose: the word that ends the answer is clued first. Both halves are innocent theatre words until they meet.
explanation.definitionFit: A show trial is staged for the public with the verdict already decided, so it is a trial in name and a performance in fact.

clue.text: Fabric of lowest quality last to be used

parts.note: the superlative of bad
the closing letter of each word that has one: bE, useD

explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' is an instruction, not part of the surface's sense of finishing a job — it picks off final letters. Worsted wool is named after Worstead in Norfolk.
explanation.definitionFit: Worsted is a smooth, tightly spun woollen yarn and the cloth woven from it, so 'fabric' names it by its general class.

clue.text: Very old person's nice tan misguided

parts.note: the seven letters of NICE TAN, re-sorted

explanation.walkthrough: The fodder hides in plain sight as a compliment about somebody's holiday. Read the definition as a noun: the answer here names a human being, not a property.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient is an aged person — the noun survives in 'the ancients' — so the definition names a human being rather than describing a thing's age.

parts.note: a zit is a spot on the skin
the possessive of 'that woman'

explanation.walkthrough: A pimple and a pronoun build a concert instrument, and the join is invisible because neither half looks like crossword material.
explanation.definitionFit: A zither is a stringed instrument played flat on a table and plucked rather than bowed, so the definition names it by its family.

parts.note: n. is the standard abbreviation for note
seven letters that join the N in the shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' is not a musical note here but the footnote abbreviation, and it is fodder rather than a piece to be placed. 'Tumbling' does the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A pashmina is a fine cashmere shawl from Kashmir, so the definition names its general kind and says nothing about the wool it is made from.

parts.note: one colour standing in for 'colourful'
an act is a performance

explanation.walkthrough: Definition first, then two everyday words. The only real work is deciding which colour 'colourful' wants, and the crossing letters settle that.
explanation.definitionFit: To redact a document is to edit it for publication, and in modern use to black out the parts nobody outside is allowed to read.

clue.text: A quantity of drug wife's swallowed: look for water

parts.note: a dose is the measured quantity you take
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.walkthrough: W for wife is one of the small abbreviations every setter keeps in the drawer, and 'swallowed' is the container signal. The colon marks the definition off.
explanation.definitionFit: To dowse is to hunt for underground springs with a forked twig or a divining rod, so the definition describes an activity rather than offering a synonym.

definitions.meaning: this half asks for a noun meaning a deep emotional bond or affection toward someone
what a paperclip is for — and the icon email borrowed for the same job

explanation.walkthrough: The link word 'for' does the hiding: it reads as part of the first definition, 'fondness for', when it is really the join between the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: An attachment is an affection you feel for somebody, and also the thing clipped to a document — which is exactly what a paperclip is for.

parts.note: a wet is a feeble sort — old public-school slang
H is the standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.walkthrough: 'Outwardly' says the feeble word goes on the outside, not that anything is removed — an easy one to misread as a deletion.
explanation.definitionFit: To whet is to sharpen — a whetstone puts an edge on a blade — so whetting an appetite stimulates it into keenness.

clue.text: Charitable society has new head, a public official

parts.note: the Rotary club, the charitable society of the high street
N for new, taking over the front and ousting the R

explanation.walkthrough: A letter is swapped, not added: the club keeps its body and loses its head. The comma before the definition reads as an ordinary pause in a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A notary is licensed by the state to witness signatures and certify documents, which is what makes them an officer acting for the general public.

parts.note: your ID is the papers you carry
lest means in case — 'lest we forget'

explanation.walkthrough: 'In case' is not a container instruction but a straight synonym, lest. Spotting that small archaic word is the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An idle machine or an idle threat is one that achieves nothing, so the superlative names whichever does least good of all.
